title: India Seeks Quick Fix as UK Flags 162.5% Bulk Scotch Duty
excerpt: Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal says officials are taking legal opinion to resolve, within days, a customs classification dispute that has pushed bulk Scotch duties above their pre-deal level.
body:
• The UK has formally raised concerns with India over an effective duty of 162.5% on bulk Scotch imports, and India's commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Monday that officials are seeking legal opinion to resolve the dispute within days.
  • The India-UK trade pact, in force since July, cut the Scotch tariff to 75%, but Indian investigators argue bulk concentrates are "compound alcoholic preparations" that attract a 150% tariff plus a consumption tax, taking the total to 162.5% — above the 150% charged before the deal.
  • More than 80 containers of bulk Scotch belonging to Pernod Ricard, Diageo and Bacardi were held at Indian ports; Agrawal said the containers have now been released.
  • For buyers: distillers had already cut Scotch prices in India when the pact took effect, and the industry says the higher levy squeezes margins and working capital until the classification question is settled.

The first major dispute under the India-UK trade agreement is over a customs label. The United Kingdom has raised concerns with New Delhi over the effective duty of 162.5% that India is now imposing on bulk Scotch imports, and India is seeking legal opinion internally to resolve the matter swiftly, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Monday, according to Reuters.

Agrawal said trade and finance ministry officials are working to resolve the issue in the next few days, in line with court decisions and India's commitments under the pact. He also said containers holding bulk Scotch had been released from Indian ports, after thousands of litres belonging to Pernod Ricard, Diageo and Bacardi were stranded in more than 80 shipping containers.

"India holds its commitment to the entire agreement in that. There is no pullback, pushback, thinking back... It is clear in our mind. It's clear in the government's mind at all levels."

— Rajesh Agrawal, Commerce Secretary, quoted by Reuters

How a 75% tariff became 162.5%

The India-UK trade agreement, which came into effect in July, halved tariffs on Scotch whisky to 75% — a headline win for Pernod Ricard and Diageo, which import bulk Scotch and blend it for India's $65 billion liquor market. But Indian investigators have argued that companies are using the wrong customs classification for bulk Scotch concentrates, which they deem raw material for blended whiskies rather than finished Scotch.

Since May, investigators argue, such imports fall under a newly created customs line for "compound alcoholic preparations," which attracts a 150% tariff. A consumption tax on top takes the full charge to 162.5%, according to a government document reviewed by Reuters and eight sources with direct knowledge of the matter, as reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. Agrawal said negotiators on both sides had been unaware of certain court cases in India relating to tariff issues, and that differences in interpretation had emerged because of past court cases.

What is at stake for the industry

About 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume arrive in bulk, and India is the biggest market for Scotch by volume. Most bulk Scotch goes into Indian-Made Foreign Liquor whiskies, blended with other spirits, which sell far below wholly imported brands. Pernod Ricard, which owns Chivas Brothers, Diageo and Indian producers including Radico Khaitan and Allied Blenders and Distillers maintain that bulk and bottled Scotch should both be taxed at 75% under the pact. Under a provisional release arrangement, importers paid duty at 75% of the goods' value up front, with the rest covered by bank guarantees — a mechanism executives said stresses working capital, particularly for smaller companies. Shares of Diageo's Indian unit and other liquor makers fell after the Reuters report, with ICICI Securities warning the higher levy could reverse the margin benefits companies expected from the pact. The Scotch Whisky Association has forecast the trade deal could boost Scotch exports to India by $1.34 billion over five years.

What happens next

Agrawal's timeline is days, not months: officials are taking legal opinion and working through the classification question against existing court decisions. The British government has repeatedly said it is working with New Delhi on the issue. Until the classification is settled, importers face the 162.5% effective charge or the cost of bank guarantees, and the price cuts consumers saw when the pact took effect remain at risk.
nri_angle: The dispute tests the India-UK pact diaspora businesses celebrated, and decides whether the Scotch price cuts Indian consumers saw in July survive.
